title: 'Flock Flocked up'

reading.body:
This is a case of an automated identification system producing a false match that was then acted on as though it were confirmed fact. The failure occurred at the front end of a traffic stop, where a camera alert about a stolen plate was treated as sufficient grounds to stop a vehicle, even though the plate image belonged to a different make and model than the vehicle it was attached to. The mismatch was visible in the alert itself, which means the error was catchable before any officer approached the car.

The second failure sits further along in the deployment, in the use of force that followed. Department policy required handlers to weigh the severity of the crime, any immediate threat, and whether a suspect was resisting or fleeing before deploying a dog. The reporting states that the driver exited with his hands up, and that the plate was later confirmed not stolen, so the predicate offence that justified the stop did not exist. Catching this would have required a human check on the alert before the stop, and a policy check on the deployment decision after it.

What is not established is whether the camera system's error was a known limitation, whether officers had any reason to doubt the alert at the time, or what disciplinary outcome, if any, will follow the investigation. An internal finding of no wrongdoing is not a finding that the alert was correct, and a dropped charge is not a finding of fault.

reports.title: Body cam of TPD officers releasing K-9 on man during traffic stop
Man speaks out after police release K-9 on him during traffic stop: 'Traumatized'
TPD investigation finds no wrongdoing in use of K-9 on man during traffic stop
Charges dropped against man Toledo Police released K-9 on during traffic stop, lawyer says

summary:
Toledo Police released body camera video showing officers drawing guns and using a K-9 on a driver during a traffic stop. The stop began after a FLOCK camera alert about a stolen plate, but the report says the alert was wrong, as the plate image matched a Chevy Malibu while appearing on a red Dodge Ram. The driver, Brandon Upchurch, got out with his hands up before officers ordered him to the ground. He was arrested and charged with resisting arrest and obstruction, and police later confirmed the plate was not stolen. He received medical attention at the scene.

Multiple Toledo Police officers are under investigation over the K-9 release. Police said they believed the driver might flee and did not know if he or a passenger had weapons. Department K-9 policy requires handlers to consider the crime's severity, any immediate threat, and whether a suspect is resisting or trying to flee before deploying a dog. The article does not say what disciplinary action or further steps will follow.
